summary: Mathematical principles of linear regression, parameter estimation via Ordinary Least Squares (OLS), and numerical optimization with Gradient Descent variants.
learning_objectives: Derive the Mean Squared Error (MSE) objective function.
Formulate Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) closed-form normal equations.
Understand batch, stochastic, and mini-batch gradient descent update rules.

topic_title: Introduction to Computer Networks & Network Core
summary: Foundational overview of computer networks, examining network infrastructure, edge versus core devices, packet transmission dynamics, and latency components.
learning_objectives: Understand the difference between the network edge and network core.
Explain packet switching vs circuit switching and multiplexing techniques.
Comprehend delays in packet-switched networks: processing, queuing, transmission, and propagation.

summary: Covers the modular layered architecture of computer networking protocols, protocol data units (PDU), header overhead, and end-to-end transmission dynamics.
learning_objectives: Differentiate the 5-layer Internet protocol stack from the 7-layer OSI model.
Understand protocol encapsulation and decapsulation with headers at each tier.
Analyze packet loss, buffer overflow, and throughput metrics.

topic_title: Computer Networks: L1 - Foundations, Physical Architecture & Network Performance
summary: Exhaustive lecture notes for Computer Networks Lecture 1: Comprehensive exploration of distributed computing reality, historical evolution, 4 network components, LAN/WAN hierarchies, Internet Exchange Points (IXPs), physical topologies, packet vs circuit switching, router architectures, and mathematical latency formulations (nodal delays, bottleneck throughput, and BDP).
learning_objectives: Understand why software engineers need computer networks and how modern distributed systems depend on network fabrics.
Trace the historical evolution of networking from manual sneakernets to ARPANET, TCP/IP, and the World Wide Web.
Categorize the four fundamental components of any network: End Devices, Transmission Links, Intermediate Devices, and Protocols.
Differentiate Network Edge systems from Network Core fabrics and analyze router control plane (Routing) vs data plane (Forwarding).
Analyze physical and logical network topologies (Bus, Star, Ring, Mesh, Tree/Hybrid) including failure modes, N(N-1)/2 wiring complexity, and scalability limits.
Compare Packet Switching vs. Circuit Switching, statistical multiplexing, and store-and-forward router behavior.
Formulate and calculate the four nodal delay components: transmission, propagation, queuing, and processing delay.
Differentiate bandwidth, throughput (bottleneck link principle), and goodput, and compute Bandwidth-Delay Product (BDP) with bit-vs-byte conversion.

topic_title: Computer Networks: L2 - Layered Architectures, OSI, TCP/IP & Encapsulation
summary: Exhaustive lecture notes for Computer Networks Lecture 2: Comprehensive deep dive into protocol standardization, the 7-Layer OSI model, the TCP/IP stack, PDU hierarchies, complete encapsulation/decapsulation workflows, byte-level header anatomy (TCP, IPv4, Ethernet II), Layer 3 router frame rewriting mechanics, addressing taxonomies, and physical transmission channel physics (Nyquist & Shannon).
learning_objectives: Explain the engineering rationale for layered network architectures (Separation of Concerns, Abstraction, Interoperability, Modularity).
Dissect all 7 layers of the OSI Reference Model and understand why Session and Presentation were consolidated into Application in modern stacks.
Master the industry-standard 4/5-layer TCP/IP protocol suite and the 'Hourglass' architectural principle.
Trace the complete Protocol Data Unit (PDU) encapsulation and decapsulation pipeline across hosts, switches, and routers.
Analyze header structures byte-by-byte: TCP (20B), IPv4 (20B), and Ethernet II (14B + 4B FCS) including the 64-byte minimum frame constraint.
Understand router Layer 3 forwarding: why IP addresses are global and immutable end-to-end while MAC addresses are hop-by-hop ephemeral.
Differentiate addressing tiers (Port, IP, MAC) and delivery modes (Unicast, Broadcast, Multicast) across collision and broadcast domains.
Calculate physical transmission channel capacity using Nyquist's formula for noiseless links and Shannon's capacity theorem for noisy links.

topic_title: Computer Networks: L3 - Ethernet Framing, ARP, IPv4 Subnetting & Addressing
summary: Exhaustive lecture notes for Computer Networks Lecture 3: Comprehensive mastery of Layer 2 Ethernet framing, switch transparent CAM learning, IP MTU fragmentation, ARP protocol mechanics and security, 32-bit IPv4 addressing, binary conversion arithmetic, historical classful breakdown, CIDR prefix mathematics, Variable Length Subnet Masking (VLSM) worked case studies, private networking, NAT/PAT, DHCP DORA handshakes, and the modern IPv6 transition.
learning_objectives: Dissect the exact anatomy of an Ethernet II frame, 48-bit MAC addressing, and the physics of the 64-byte minimum frame size.
Master the switch transparent MAC learning algorithm and distinguish switch CAM forwarding tables from host ARP tables.
Understand Maximum Transmission Unit (MTU) constraints, Jumbo Frames, and calculate multi-fragment IP packet fragmentation offsets.
Explain the complete Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) workflow, message format, caching dynamics, and spoofing/poisoning security mitigations.
Convert 32-bit IPv4 addresses between binary bitstreams and dotted-decimal notation rapidly using 8-bit positional weights.
Critique historical Classful addressing (Classes A, B, C, D, E) and explain why CIDR (Classless Inter-Domain Routing) was required.
Formulate and calculate subnet boundaries: Network ID, Broadcast ID, Usable Host Range, and host capacity using 2^H - 2.
Execute Variable Length Subnet Masking (VLSM) designs by allocating largest host blocks first and eliminating address space fragmentation.
Differentiate RFC 1918 private address ranges, special addresses (Loopback, APIPA, Default Route), and Network Address Translation (NAT/PAT).
Trace the 4-step DHCP DORA handshake and dissect IPv6 128-bit structure, zero-compression rules, and prefix classifications.
